Title: Go To Hellman: Authors are Not People: ORCID and the Challenges of Name Disambiguation
### Authors are Not People: ORCID and the Challenges of Name Disambiguation. In December, a group of organizations led by Thomson Reuters (owners of the Web of Knowledge service that is the descendent of the Science Citation Index) and the Nature Publishing Group announced (pdf, 15kB) the creation of an effort to create unique identifiers for scientific authors. Named ORCID, for Open Researcher & Contributor ID, the organization will try to turn Thomson Reuters' Researcher ID system into an open, self-sustaining non-profit service for the scholarly publishing, research and education communities. For example, in a recent study we chose 100 names of MEDLINE authors at random, and then a pair of articles was randomly chosen for each name; these pairs were disambiguated manually, using additional information as necessary and available (e.g., author or institutional homepages, the full-text of the articles, Community of Science profiles (http://www.cos.com), Google searches, etc.). The remaining approach to the author name problem is to involve the authoring community, which is the thrust of the ORCID project. Surely authors themselves know best how to disambiguate their names from others! The group charged with developing ORCID's business model are currently looking at memberships and grants as the most likely source of funds, recognizing that the necessity for broad author participation precludes author fees as a revenue source. ORCID commercial participants hope to use ORCID data to pull costs out of their own processes, to fuel social networks for authors or to drive new or existing information services. Libraries and research foundations hope to use ORCID data to improve information access, faculty rankings and grant administration processes. results.content:
Title: Author Name Disambiguation Techniques | Nature Research Intelligence
# Author Name Disambiguation Techniques. Author name disambiguation represents a critical challenge in contemporary bibliometrics and digital library management. More recent strategies integrate rule-based systems, machine learning algorithms and graph models that utilise bibliographic metadata to construct more nuanced and adaptable disambiguation techniques. Such advances have not only enhanced the accuracy and efficiency of disambiguation systems but have also increased their applicability across diverse digital repositories, enabling more precise author-level analyses and supporting the integrity of scholarly communication. Recent investigations in the field have explored both enhanced supervised classifiers and sophisticated unsupervised clustering algorithms to overcome challenges posed by ambiguous author names. For instance, researchers have refined pair-wise similarity approaches by incorporating additional features such as email addresses, affiliations and nuanced coauthor networks [1]. In parallel, comparative studies of various unsupervised methods have demonstrated that a meticulous calibration of clustering parameters significantly increases disambiguation accuracy, especially when dealing with large-scale bibliometric data sets [3]. Moreover, the construction and empirical analysis of curated data sets have allowed for a more rigorous validation of these methods, thereby pushing forward the state-of-the-art in reliable author identification [4]. **Supervised classification:** A machine learning technique where the algorithm is trained on labelled examples to learn the relationship between input features and target outputs. **Unsupervised clustering:** A method for grouping data points based on intrinsic similarities without prior labelling, often used to detect patterns in large data sets. **Pair-wise similarity metrics:** Quantitative measures used to assess the degree of similarity between two data points, such as two author records. **Graph-based approaches:** Techniques that represent entities and their relationships in a network structure, aiding in the visualisation and resolution of complex association patterns between authors. ## Author Name Disambiguation Techniques Publication Trend.
